Learning Objectives
Review the history of technology in total hip arthroplasty.
Review the preoperative requirements for various technologies used in total hip arthroplasty.
Explain the technical and procedural differences among modern handheld navigation,
computer-assisted surgery, and robot-assisted surgery.
History
Computer navigation and robot-assisted techniques have emerged in an attempt to improve
the accuracy and reproducibility of implant positioning during total hip arthroplasty (THA).

Optimal implant position is crucial to ensure high function and long-term survivorship and to
minimize the risk of instability and bearing wear.1-3

History
Various systems have been developed to more accurately place implants during THA
(Table 1). The first forms of computer navigation were console-based navigation systems
that were imageless, meaning that they were not dependent on preoperative imaging
but on intraoperative bony registration to establish a relative reference frame for the
pelvis and femur. An array was placed on the iliac crest to register the pelvis, and a
checkpoint was placed on the femur to register hip length and offset. Console-based
navigation systems were not largely adopted because of their large size, cost, line-of-
sight visualization issues between the camera and the arrays/probe, and concerns
regarding accuracy.
To address the shortcomings of console-based computer navigation, smaller pelvic-
mounted navigation systems were developed. These devices generally are easier to use
because they are smaller and do not have the line-of-sight issues associated with the
console navigation systems. Various pelvic-mounted technologies are available. The two
pelvic-mounted technologies discussed in this lesson are a pelvic-mounted handheld
accelerometer-based device and a pelvic-mounted infrared miniature camera. Both of
these systems aid in acetabular positioning and provide feedback on hip length and
offset.
Robotic systems have been developed and have gained interest. In general, robotic
systems require preoperative imaging studies to match the patient’s preoperative bony
anatomy to the patient’s position in three-dimensional space during surgery. Robot-
assisted surgery has been defined as fully active or semi-active, depending on the
degree to which it permits the surgeon to retain some control over the task. The first
robotic device for total joint arthroplasty, the ROBODOC system (Curexo Technology),
was introduced in 1985.4,5 It is a CT-based computer-aided robotic milling device
originally designed to facilitate femoral component preparation and implantation. In this
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:15 AM

system, the preoperative plan is created using the ORTHODOC software, which creates a
three-dimensional virtual model of the patient’s anatomy based on preoperative CT
scans. This plan is then transferred to the ROBODOC surgical assistant, which completes
all reaming, broaching, and positioning of the final implants. The surgeon can oversee
the robot and activate an emergency stop button but does not directly control the robot.
Studies have demonstrated some improvements in component radiographic parameters
and good outcomes associated with the fully active ROBODOC system;6-9 however,
adoption has been limited because it is a time-consuming process that many surgeons
feel is cumbersome.

Alternatively, semi-active systems gained attention because they are more user friendly
by providing active constraint, in which the surgeon has control over the surgical process
but receives haptic feedback intraoperatively. A popular semi-active robot is the Mako
robot-assisted haptic arm (Stryker). The robotic arm allows the surgeon to perform the
surgical procedure but is guided by the haptic boundaries that limit deviations in bone
preparation and implantation from the preprogrammed plan. The system has proved to
be very accurate for cup positioning and hip length and offset.10-15 Given that CT is
performed preoperatively, advanced planning can be performed to account for
individual anatomy and pelvic positioning. Impingement modeling is performed in
various positions, including supine, sitting, and standing, to help identify areas of
impingement and to optimize reconstruction. Some early studies have shown that
results of robotic hip replacement are improved; however, larger and longer studies are
necessary.16-18

Computer navigation systems and robot-assisted THA have demonstrated improvement
in implant positioning and restoration of the hip center, hip length, and offset while
minimizing outliers.10-15,19-22 A potential advantage of navigation or robotics in THA is a
reduction in acetabular component positioning outliers. The concept of an acetabular
safe zone is appealing but likely too simplistic and does not account for many other
variables that are important during THA. Traditional teaching was that acetabular cups
outside the Lewinnek safe zone, which is 5° to 25° of anteversion and 30° to 50° of
abduction, were at increased risk for instability;23-25 however, larger studies have
disproved an absolute safe zone that can be applied to all patients, and more discussion
has centered on individualized implant positioning.26,27
Although a universal safe zone may not exist, surgeons should have targets for
reconstruction. Multiple large retrospective studies have demonstrated that with
conventional freehand techniques, only 51% to 85% of cups are implanted within a
targeted zone.20,25 Although few studies have directly compared computer-navigated
nonrobotic THA with robotic THA, studies have shown that navigated and robotically
placed cups were more likely to be within a targeted zone than those placed during
conventional THA.10-15,19-22 As additional knowledge is gained, these technologies may
allow surgeons to hit patient-specific targets rather than general target ranges.
Handheld Navigation
HipAlign (OrthAlign) is an accelerometer-based handheld device composed of a reference
sensor and a disposable computer display. Accelerometer-based navigation systems have
been shown to be associated with excellent accuracy in total knee arthroplasty and recently
have been available for THA. For THA, HipAlign has shown early promising accuracy, along with
a short learning time and minimal time required for use.21,22 A posterolateral approach can be
used; an anterior supine-based surgical approach platform also is available.
Preoperative Planning
HipAlign is an imageless navigation system that does not require any additional preoperative
imaging (Figure 1).

Preoperative planning and templating are encouraged for acetabular and femoral positioning
and implant fit and sizing but are not necessary for this navigation system.
Figure 1
Image shows HipAlign (OrthAlign) system components. (Courtesy of Seth A. Jerabek, MD, New
York, NY.)
Patient Positioning
The patient is positioned in the lateral decubitus position for the posterolateral approach, with
the pelvis secured to minimize motion intraoperatively.
Careful level positioning of the pelvis is critical for initial reference of pelvic positioning.
The iliac crest and the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) must be prepared and accessible
intraoperatively because identification of the iliac crest and the ASIS is required for proper
placement of the pins and mounting of the device.
Initial Registration and Pin Placement
Pelvic registration is performed before the hip approach.

Two pins are placed in the iliac crest, and the device is attached to these pins.
Proper placement of these pins is crucial, identifying both sides of the iliac crest, and the
inner and outer table; mark if necessary.
Make two small incisions just through the skin with the use of a No. 11 blade. The first
incision should be approximately three to four fingerbreadths posterior to the ASIS on top of
the iliac crest. Use a blunt device to spread down to the iliac crest (tonsil, snap). The first
incision should be made, after which the base is used to measure how far posterior the
second incision should be placed.
The base is placed onto both pins and secured.
The HipAlign screen is attached to the pins and base
Initial selection screen: select as appropriate (Figure 2)
Figure 2
Images show the initial selection screens (top) and registration of anatomic landmarks (bottom)
for total hip arthroplasty with the use of the HipAlign (OrthAlign) system. After the pins are placed
into the iliac crest and the base is attached to the pins, the screen is mounted to the base and
ready for initial registration. The surgeon selects Hip, the approach, laterality, and patient sex.
(Courtesy of Seth A. Jerabek, MD, New York, NY.)

Femoral Registration
Femoral registration is performed before dislocation of the hip.
A checkpoint is placed on the lateral aspect of the greater trochanter, approximately two to
three fingerbreadths distal from the tip of the greater trochanter.
A bump is placed under the knee of the surgical leg, and a laser crosshair is pointed toward a
removable magnetic plate placed on the knee.
The probe tip is placed in the center of the checkpoint, and registration is recorded with the
HipAlign system. The location of the laser crosshair is marked on the removable magnetic
plate with the use of a marking pen at the time of checkpoint registration. The plate is then
removed and stored for use at the end of the procedure to determine postoperative leg
length and offset.
Pelvic Registration
The registration system involves referencing the following:
Pelvic position on the surgical table
Anterior pelvic plane
Performed before hip exposure
After HipAlign is attached to the iliac crest pins, the coronal plane of the pelvis is registered.
The probe is extended from the base, oriented parallel with the surgical table and in line with
the coronal plane of the pelvis (Figure 3, A).

Surgical Exposure

In the example discussed in this lesson, a posterolateral surgical exposure is performed;
however, an anterior workflow also is available.
Setting the Cup Position
The surgeon can enhance inclination precision using preoperative radiographic information.
Set the preferred target angles for cup inclination and anteversion on the HipAlign screen.
With the sensor attached to the impaction handle, impact the acetabular component (Figure
3, C)
Live acetabular component position numbers are shown on the device during impaction of the
component.
Inclination and anteversion are shown.
Femoral Preparation
Femoral preparation is performed.
During trial reduction, the magnetic plate used during femoral registration is placed back on
the leg near the knee. The leg is then held in a position in which the crosshair laser matches
the marking pen lines placed previously. The pointer probe is placed in the checkpoint on the
femur, and the registration button is clicked. This provides the change in leg length and offset
(Figure 3, D).
Depending on target hip length and offset of the surgical leg, the surgeon may make changes
in the femoral component, offset, or neck length to optimize reconstruction.
This step can be repeated with final implants in place before removal of the femoral
checkpoint to gain final change in hip length and offset.
Computer-Assisted Surgery

Computer-Assisted Surgery
Intellijoint HIP (Intellijoint Surgical) is an imageless navigation system that uses a pelvic-
mounted miniature infrared camera and a navigation device that has internal inertial
sensors and microelectronics to aid in THA. It provides feedback on the hip center of
rotation, cup orientation, leg length, and offset. It does not reference the anterior pelvic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Advanced Technologies in Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004022
10/26

plane; therefore, registration is simple but very dependent on precise pelvic positioning
intraoperatively. Several small studies assessing the accuracy and efficiency of the
Intellijoint HIP have reported encouraging early results.28-30 A direct anterior supine
approach is discussed in this lesson; however, a lateral decubitus–based approach
workflow also is available.
Preoperative Planning
Intellijoint HIP is an imageless navigation system that uses a pelvic-mounted infrared camera.
Preoperative planning and templating are encouraged for acetabular and femoral positioning
and for implant fit and sizing but not necessary for this navigation system.
Patient Positioning
This system can be used for surgical procedures in the supine and lateral decubitus positions.
The case discussed in this lesson is THA via the direct anterior approach with the patient in the
supine position.
Sterile skin preparation is carried to just cephalad to the level of the umbilicus.
Draping must allow for access to the ASIS and the anterior half of the iliac crest for pin
placement.
Registration
Pin insertion—Mark the ASIS and the inner and outer tables of the iliac crest. The pins can be
placed on the contralateral or the surgical side.
Using a knife with a No. 11 blade, make an approximately 1-cm incision 1 cm posterior to the
ASIS along the iliac crest.
Use the platform guide to measure how far posterior the second incision should be made.
Again, using a knife with a No. 11 blade, make a stab incision for the second pin site centered
over the iliac crest.
Insert the first partially threaded pin by hand and feel the inner and outer tables of the iliac
crest; ensure placement centered on the iliac crest between the inner and outer tables, use a
mallet to engage the pin tip into the bone, and then use power to drive the pin in so that the
threads engage and the pin is stable. Repeat with the second, more posterior pin.

Place the camera onto the platform.
Adjust the camera position while looking at the intraoperative screen on the Intellijoint HIP
monitor until the camera field of view is optimized for the procedure.
Register the horizontal plane, and select hip laterality (Figure 4, A).

Surgical Exposure
Femoral checkpoint placement—After the surgical approach is performed, the femur is
internally rotated slightly, and a femoral checkpoint is inserted on the anterolateral aspect of
the greater trochanter at a level just distal to the vastus ridge. Clear off soft tissue
approximately 1 × 1 cm down to bone to make room for the femoral checkpoint.
The femoral array base is secured with the use of a screw.
Femoral Registration
Using the probe with the array, place in the center of the checkpoint to register the femur
Calibrate the probe by placing it on solid bone around the femoral neck and moving it in small
circles (Figure 4, B)
Register the surgical ASIS, then the nonsurgical ASIS, and the pubis in the supine position with
the tip of the probe
Software will calculate pelvic tilt (Figure 4, C).
Baseline leg length—Place the probe on the femoral checkpoint on the outer rim. With the tip
of the probe engaged in the outer rim, sweep the tip of the probe around the checkpoint rim
until the screen icon turns completely green (Figure 4, D).
Acetabular Registration
After registration of baseline leg length and offset, the femoral neck may be osteotomized
based on the surgeon’s preferred technique and templating.
Leave the native femoral head in the acetabulum and use the corkscrew driver to engage into
the center of the femoral head.
Baseline hip center—Attach the magnetic array to the corkscrew handle, and with pressure
against the handle to keep the femoral head against the acetabulum, make small to moderate-
sized circles, ensuring that the camera can visualize the array to determine hip center of
rotation (Figure 4, E).
Acetabular preparation—Prepare the acetabulum based on surgeon preference and the
preoperative template if desired. Surgeons may prefer to use intraoperative fluoroscopy
during the direct anterior approach for acetabular reaming and/or initial cup positioning.
Acetabular component positioning—After acetabular reaming is complete, begin to impact the
acetabular component.

Place the magnetic array on the cup impactor to evaluate the cup orientation and adjust in
real time with feedback from the screen based on target goals (Figure 4, F).
Confirm cup orientation on the Intellijoint screen (Figure 4, G).
Liner insertion—Insert and engage the liner into the locking mechanism.
Obtain new hip center—With the liner impactor retained in the liner, place the magnetic array
on the liner impactor and make small to moderate-sized circles to obtain new hip center
(Figure 4, H).
After the new center of rotation is obtained, the software will determine the change in center
of rotation relative to the superior/inferior, anterior/posterior, and medial/lateral positions
(Figure 4, I).
Femoral Preparation
Femoral stem preparation is performed based on surgeon protocol.
After femoral preparation is complete, reduce the trial broach with the desired neck and head,
and assess clinically for stability and soft-tissue tension.
Femoral checkpoint registration—Use the probe on the outer engraved rim of the femoral
checkpoint to evaluate leg length and offset.
Final registration—Implant the final femoral component and use the femoral checkpoint and
probe with array in the same manner to assess final leg length and offset (Figure 4, J).
Surgeons also may use intraoperative fluoroscopy with the anterior approach to confirm
femoral component positioning, size, and leg length and offset.
Robot-Assisted Surgery

Robot-Assisted Surgery
The most commonly used robotics platform, the Mako robot-assisted haptic arm
(Stryker), is CT-based, which allows for preoperative planning in three dimensions and
allows the surgeon to account for the patient’s anatomy for the acetabular and femoral
components. In addition, the patient’s functional pelvic position in the supine, sitting,
and standing positions can be analyzed, and simulated range of motion and
impingement profiles can be determined preoperatively. Intraoperatively, the bone is
registered by taking a series of points with a probe, which is matched to the CT scan,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Advanced Technologies in Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004022
16/26

enabling the robot to know the location of the bone is in space. A robotic arm is then
used to prepare the acetabulum and to position and impact the acetabular component.
Femoral reconstruction is performed by the surgeon with the use broaches; however,
the system allows the surgeon to determine hip length, offset, and version.
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative CT: includes the entire pelvis, bilateral proximal femurs, and sections through the
distal femurs (condylar axis) for version calculation
Preoperative sitting and standing cross pelvic radiographs may be used to determine pelvic
position in these functional positions and allow for impingement modeling. Pelvic tilt typically
is measured using the anterior pelvic plane or the sacral slope (Figure 5, A).
Three-dimensional planning
Acetabular positioning—Dependent on anatomy and goals of combined anteversion and
offset. The default cup abduction is 40° and anteversion is 20°. The cup orientation may be
altered to account for pelvic anatomy and/or femoral version and impingement. The hip
center of rotation may be modified in all three planes: transverse, sagittal, and coronal
(medial/lateral, cephalad/caudad, anterior/posterior; Figure 5, B).
Femoral component—The optimal stem choice and size is based on proximal femoral
geometry, femoral version, and offset. Native femoral version and planned stem version are
displayed. Reconstruction is compared with the native anatomy and the contralateral side
(Figure 5, C).
Impingement modeling—After the standing and sitting pelvic positions are entered and the
acetabular and femoral components have been planned, impingement modeling can be
performed. The plan may be adjusted to optimize reconstruction (Figure 5, D).
Simulated radiographic verification—A simulated radiograph can be viewed preoperatively.
This radiograph accurately represents what the radiograph will look like postoperatively
(Figure 5, E).

Patient Positioning
Lateral decubitus
Used for posterolateral, anterolateral, and direct superior approaches
Preparation and draping to allow for full exposure of the ASIS and most of the iliac crest
Supine
Used for the direct anterior approach
Preparation and draping to allow for full exposure of the ASIS and most of the iliac crest
The array may be placed on the surgical iliac crest or the nonsurgical iliac crest.
Marker distally on the surgical leg—An electrocardiographic lead is placed just superior to the
distal pole of the patella as a reference point for leg length.
Registration
Robot registration—The robotic arm and the probe are registered for accuracy of less than 1
mm preoperatively.
Surgical Exposure
Surgical exposure is based on surgeon preference. Workflows are available for all major
approaches to the hip.
Pelvic array placement—The array requires three pins in the iliac crest. The pins should be
placed between the inner and outer tables of the iliac crest posterior to the ASIS. The pins

Express versus enhanced workflows
Enhanced workflow allows for femoral registration points and guided neck cut and provides
intraoperative femoral version.
Acetabular Registration and Preparation
The pelvic checkpoint is inserted just superior to the acetabulum to verify array accuracy.
Multiple bony points are taken using a probe within and surrounding the acetabulum (Figure
5, F).
Acetabular reaming—The reamer is attached to the robotic arm and functions within a haptic
cone/boundary. The reamer is constrained within a finite determined space based on the
planned hip center, inclination, and version (Figure 5, G).
The remainder of the reamer arm is permitted to move within the conical area to remove the
predetermined amount of bone based on reamer size.
Option—Single reaming of the size compatible for the acetabular component
Acetabular component placement—The acetabular component is attached to the end of the
robotic arm via an inserter.
Verify final registration, then impact the cup.
Cup insertion occurs with haptics, which does not allow for deviation from predetermined
orientation or depth.
After the cup is placed, acquire five points around the rim of the acetabular component using
the probe. Final orientation is obtained and typically is the same as that determined in the
preoperative plan; however, small deviations may occur, especially in patients with
sclerotic/hard bone.
Insert the respective chosen liner and impact into the cup; ensure that the locking mechanism
is engaged appropriately.
Femoral Registration (Express and Enhanced) and Preparation
Express Workflow
Uses two-point registration with a checkpoint in the lateral greater trochanter and an
electrocardiographic lead at the distal pole of the patella to register preoperative hip length
and offset (Figure 5, H).

The hip is dislocated, and the neck cut is performed based on preoperative templating.
The femur is prepared manually according to preoperative plan.
After the acetabulum is prepared, the trial femur and head are reduced.
The two original points (greater trochanter checkpoint and electrocardiographic lead on the
patella) are registered, and the system provides feedback on hip length and offset.
Adjustments may be made at this point, or final implants may be placed (Figure 5, I).
Express workflow does not provide femoral version or a guided neck cut.
Enhanced Workflow
The hip is dislocated.
An array mounting screw is placed between the greater trochanter and the lesser trochanter
and a checkpoint (Figure 5, J).
The femur is registered by taking multiple points using a probe on the proximal femur, as
dictated by computer software (Figure 5, K).
After the femur is registered, the probe can be used to plan a guided femoral neck cut
osteotomized at the level of the preoperative plan (Figure 5, L).
Femoral preparation—Ream-and-broach or broach-only techniques may be used based on
stem choice and surgeon preference.
Hip length, offset, and femoral version—Leave the femoral broach in place, put a trial femoral
neck in place, and take three points from divots in the femoral neck (Figure 5, M)
Based on the results, the surgeon may adjust the plan or place the final implants (Figure 5,
N).
Adjustments to cup orientation (increasing/decreasing anteversion), liner choice, etc.
Changes to femoral implant size, offset, and head lengths can be made to optimize hip
length and offset.
Hip Reduction and Trialing
Intraoperative stability testing is critically important regardless of the reconstruction numbers.
The surgeon must ensure hip stability intraoperatively.

Conclusion
Because a universal safe zone does not exist, THA is moving in the direction of patient-
specific functional planning. As surgeons account for more variables, such as spinopelvic
mobility, bony morphology, femoral anteversion, combined anteversion, and combined
offset, patient-specific targets likely will become narrower. Enabling technologies are
proved to be more accurate than freehand hip replacement.
Handheld navigation, pelvic-mounted computer-assisted surgery, and robot-assisted
THA currently are the most commonly used enabling technologies. Handheld navigation
and pelvic-mounted computer-assisted surgery involve relatively small devices that are
easy to use, can accurately hit targets, and do not require preoperative imaging studies;
however, they do not currently provide advanced planning tools. Robot-assisted hip
replacement provides more information because of preoperative CT, which also allows
for functional assessment and impingement modeling in the supine, standing, and
sitting positions. Larger studies and longer follow-up are necessary to determine
whether these technologies will provide a substantial clinical benefit or be worth the
additional expense.
